questions.q: A screenwriter's hero is decent but dull, and test readers don't mind what happens to him. Which of Hauge's tools would add sympathy most directly?
choices: Give him a clearer dramatic question
Show him suffering a misfortune he did nothing to deserve
Add a Midpoint false victory
Make his first line on the nose
questions.explain: Hauge's sympathy comes from undeserved misfortune; the word 'undeserved' is what makes it work.

questions.q: Which of these best states Emma Coats's rule #1?
choices: Every scene must turn a value
Characters should surprise us convincingly
We admire a character for trying more than for their successes
Kill your darlings
questions.explain: Effort draws us in more than success. The other options belong to McKee, Forster and the 'murder your darlings' advice.

questions.q: In Rocky (1976), Rocky is sent to break a debtor's thumb and doesn't. What is this moment doing?
choices: Kicking the dog, marking him as a villain
Delivering the inciting incident
Planting a MacGuffin
Petting the dog: a small kindness that tells us a hard man has a softer side
questions.explain: It's a pet-the-dog touch, and a good one because it grows out of who he is: he isn't really cut out for the life he's living.

questions.q: Sherlock Holmes is rude and cold, yet readers follow him eagerly. Which source of investment is mainly at work?
choices: Competence: the pleasure of watching someone be superb at something
Jeopardy
Undeserved misfortune
Worse people around him
questions.explain: Power or skill is one of Hauge's tools, and it can carry characters who aren't likable at all.

questions.q: A writer says: 'My protagonist is a manipulative schemer, so no one will follow her.' What's the best reply?
choices: Add a save-the-cat scene and make her nice
Switch to a different protagonist
Caring isn't liking: fascination, competence or worse people around her can hold an audience
Cut her scenes down so she's less present
questions.explain: Investment doesn't require approval. Richard III and Tom Ripley hold us through fascination and skill.

questions.q: A villain's first scene shows him casually ordering puppies turned into coats. What's the technique?
choices: Pet the dog
Status details
Undeserved misfortune
Kick the dog: a gratuitous cruelty that tells the audience where they stand
questions.explain: Kick the dog marks a villain with one cruel act, as Cruella de Vil's plan does.

questions.q: A feature writer's draft calls a family's situation 'heartbreaking' four times, but editors say it feels cold. What would this lesson suggest?
choices: Cut the telling words and show, in concrete detail, what the family is trying to do and what's in the way
Add more adjectives to make the feeling clearer
Open with a statistic
Move the family to the end of the piece
questions.explain: Care for real people comes from specificity and visible wanting, not from adjectives that instruct the reader to feel.

questions.q: Breaking Bad opens with Walter White underpaid, humiliated and diagnosed with cancer. In terms of audience sympathy, what is the series doing?
choices: Using jeopardy alone
Buying sympathy with undeserved misfortune early, then spending it as he becomes a monster
Following Snyder's Midpoint rule
Avoiding identification altogether
questions.explain: Sympathy is a credit the story can spend; the early misfortune keeps us with Walt long after we stop approving of him.

ideas: Identification, the audience stepping into the hero's shoes, comes from tools like undeserved misfortune, jeopardy, likability, humor and skill.
Caring about a character is not the same as liking them: fascination and competence can hold us just as well.
We judge characters on a curve, so surrounding a bad protagonist with worse people moves our sympathy toward them.
Early sympathy is a credit that a story can spend as its hero grows darker.
